title: This Robot Bird Can Fly — and Swim Underwater
summary:
Diving birds, such as Atlantic puffins, do not use their wings just for flying. They also use them to swim underwater and chase prey. Inspired by these birds, a team of scientists led by Raphael Zufferey of MIT has created a robot that does the same thing.

The lightweight robot is called the FAAV, short for flapping-wing aerial-aquatic vehicle. It uses its wings to move smoothly between flying and swimming. Building a machine that can move through both air and water was no easy task. Water is about 1,000 times denser than air, so moving through it requires much more force. Birds can fold their wings to help them swim, but adding a folding mechanism would make a small robot more complicated. To solve this, the team gave the robot flexible wings that bend up to 90 degrees when pushing through water.

Next, the scientists had to find the best wing size. They tested three different sizes and found that medium-sized wings offered a good balance. They bent enough to work underwater while still providing the lift needed for flight. To help the wings shed water after swimming, they were coated with tiny, water-repelling particles. This kept them light enough for takeoff.

In tests, the robot swam underwater at nearly 3 feet (1 meter) per second and flew at about 20 feet (6 meters) per second. These speeds were similar to those of real diving birds. Also, unlike most diving birds, the robot did not need to paddle its feet to get airborne. It rose out of the water and took off using only its wings.

The team published its findings in the journal Science on July 9, 2026. The researchers are now working to improve the wings so they can turn as well as flap up and down. They also plan to test the robot in choppy water and windy conditions. Once ready, the robot could help scientists study the ocean more efficiently.

"One of the major challenges in ocean science is collecting data both frequently and across many locations, which is something this robot could do in the future," Zufferey says. "You could send this out not just every week, but every hour. It could fly out at high speeds, dive in, fly back, deliver its data, and go back out, multiple times."
why_it_matters: A robot that can fly and swim could help scientists gather ocean data far more often and from far more places, which matters because the ocean is huge, hard to reach, and key to understanding our planet.

background_read: Some seabirds, like puffins, are built for two worlds: they fly through the air and also 'fly' underwater, using their wings to chase fish.
Engineers often copy nature when they design machines, because animals have already solved hard problems like moving smoothly or saving energy.
A machine that can both fly and swim could be useful for ocean science, since much of the sea is hard to reach and study from a boat or from shore.
The hard part is that air and water are very different: water pushes back far more strongly, so a wing that works well in one may fail in the other.

KEY EVENT: The team created the FAAV, a lightweight robot inspired by diving birds like Atlantic puffins.

├─ CHALLENGE: Water is about 1,000 times denser than air, so moving through it takes much more force.

└─ RESULTS: It swam at nearly 3 feet per second and flew at about 20 feet per second, like real diving birds, and took off without paddling.
EVIDENCE: The team published its findings in the journal Science on July 9, 2026.
